sentences.text: 51 Pegasi b.
In nineteen ninety-five Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz noticed that this Sun-like star was wobbling slightly: an invisible planet was tugging at it.
This giant, half as massive as Jupiter, is seven times closer to its star than Mercury is to the Sun, and one orbit takes only four days.
No one expected anything like this; gas giants were supposed to be far away and slow, like Jupiter.
The concept of the hot Jupiter was born that night.
Twenty-four years later this discovery won the Nobel Prize in Physics.
55 Cancri e, forty-one light-years away; its star can be seen with the naked eye.
A super-Earth nearly twice Earth's diameter and eight times its mass.
But its year lasts only seventeen hours.
It is so close to its star that one face always points toward it, and the dayside is a lava ocean molten at two thousand degrees.
Compare it with Earth: about twice as wide, but wrapped in minerals vaporized from rock.
In twenty twenty-four the Webb telescope detected a thick atmosphere here made of carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide; an atmosphere the lava ocean breathes out.
HD 189733 b, sixty-four light-years away.
The first exoplanet whose color was measured: from the light it reflects, Hubble found that it is a deep cobalt blue.
But this blue does not come from oceans.
Silicate grains, that is, particles of glass, float in its atmosphere and scatter the light blue, like Earth's sky.
The temperature is close to a thousand degrees, and the winds reach eight thousand kilometers per hour.
Here the rain falls sideways, and it is made of glass.
HD 209458 b, nicknamed Osiris.
In nineteen ninety-nine it became the first planet caught passing in front of its star: the star's light dimmed by one and a half percent every three and a half days.
You are watching that very moment right now; the planet is in front of its star like a silhouette.
This tiny dimming is the very method that let the Kepler and TESS space telescopes find thousands of worlds.
During a transit, starlight filters through the planet's atmosphere, and Hubble found traces of sodium, hydrogen, and oxygen in that light.
The planet is so hot that its atmosphere is escaping into space like a comet; ten thousand tons every second.
HD 80606 b, on an orbit with no equal in the Solar System.
Its eccentricity is zero point ninety-three: at its farthest from its star, nearly as far as Earth, at its closest, only a tenth as far as Mercury's orbit.
It spends most of its one hundred eleven day orbit in the cold, then shoots past its star like a comet.
The Spitzer telescope watched this passage: the atmosphere heated from five hundred degrees to one thousand two hundred degrees in six hours.
After the passage, planet-wide storms form at several times the speed of sound.
The distant companion star HD 80007 probably pushed it into this orbit.
Welcome to the exoplanet tour.
Thirty years ago we did not know of even a single planet outside the Solar System; today we know nearly six thousand worlds.
On this tour we will fly to eight stars and look at what we found there: a planet where it rains glass, a gas giant close enough to touch its star, a tiny family of seven rocky worlds.
Everything you will see is based on real measurements: orbits, sizes, and temperatures.
The surfaces, though, are the computer's estimate.
Fasten your seat belts; our first star is fifty light-years away.
KELT-9 b: the hottest planet known.
Its star is nearly twice as hot as the Sun, a blue-white A-type star, and the planet is close enough to complete one orbit of it every thirty-six hours.
The dayside reaches four thousand six hundred kelvin; that is hotter than many stars.
At that temperature molecules break apart: water and carbon dioxide cannot exist, and the atmosphere is filled with atomic iron and titanium vapor.
The star's ultraviolet radiation melts thousands of tons off the planet every second.
What's more, its orbit passes over the poles of its star; like a comet turning the wrong way.
Our last stop: Kepler-452 b, about one thousand eight hundred light-years away.
Its star is nearly the Sun's twin; a little older, a little brighter.
The planet is as far from its star as we are from the Sun, and its year is three hundred eighty-five days.
Sixty percent wider than Earth; whether it is rocky, or carries a thick envelope of gas, we do not know.
When it was discovered, it was called Earth's big, old cousin.
On this world, one and a half billion years older, if there is life, its slowly brightening star is scorching it before us: a window opening onto Earth's future.
Six thousand planets, in thirty years.
None of them is yet a second Earth; but each one tells us a little more about how unusual we are, or how ordinary.
The exoplanet tour has ended.
Kepler-90, two thousand eight hundred light-years away; a star similar to the Sun, and exactly eight planets.
Tied with the Solar System: the most crowded planetary system known.
Its layout resembles ours too: small rocky worlds on the inside, gas giants on the outside.
The difference is that all of them fit inside Earth's orbit; the outermost, Kepler-90 h, is as far from its star as we are from the Sun, and Jupiter-sized.
The eighth planet, Kepler-90 i, was found in twenty seventeen, when a neural network from Google scanned a faint signal in the Kepler data: the first machine-learning discovery.
This packed system tells us that planets can migrate inward after they are born.
And our nearest neighbor.
Proxima Centauri b, around the closest star to the Sun, four point two light-years away.
Earth-mass and in the habitable zone; it completes one orbit of its star every eleven days.
But its star is a cranky red dwarf: its flares spew hundreds of times the radiation Earth sees, and may already have stripped the planet's atmosphere.
The star is deep crimson and huge in the sky, but the daylight is only sixty-five percent of Earth's.
Recently a second planet was confirmed in the same system: Proxima d, lighter than Mars.
With our fastest probe today, the journey here would take seventy thousand years; Breakthrough Starshot's laser sails dream of bringing that down to twenty years.
TRAPPIST-1: forty light-years away, a cold red dwarf only a little larger than Jupiter.
And around it, seven Earth-sized rocky planets.
All of them are closer to the star than Mercury is to the Sun; the outermost completes one orbit in only nineteen days.
Three are in the habitable zone: e, f, and g.
You are now above e; neighboring planet f appears as large as the Moon in the sky, the planets are so close to one another that you could make out the continents.
The star stands deep red, and four times as wide as the Sun covers in our sky.
The Webb telescope is measuring these worlds' atmospheres one by one; it found no thick atmosphere on the innermost two.
Now it is e's turn.
